a.xlink:title: Nebi publishes and imports workspace bundles through any OCI registry, with Artifact Keeper serving as another configured registry rather than a new capability. Every push creates a content-addressed tag with the `sha-` prefix, `latest`, and any user tags. A bundle carries `pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock`, and optional source, README, or data layers; it carries the spec rather than a materialized environment, so each consumer still runs `pixi install`. Nebi does not yet support the `tool.pixi` tables in `pyproject.toml` manifests.

a.xlink:title: Building the materialized environment into a container image ahead of cluster launch lets each worker pull and run without an environment-materialization step. This mechanism pays image-pull time per node rather than install time per pod. It is the preferred direction rather than an agreed one, and it assumes a registry every user can publish to, which depends on the unresolved question of whether Artifact Keeper belongs in the core deployment.

a.xlink:title: Object storage supports concurrent multi-node access and is the preferred medium for large datasets and immutable artifacts.
The DSP group-directory contract requires multi-node read-write access.

Whether Ray has a file-broadcast equivalent to Dask's has not been confirmed.

a.xlink:title: A node-group disk resize encounters the instance-manager PDB while the node holds the final replica. Maintenance therefore requires replica movement or an explicit relaxation of the data-safety policy.

Longhorn reserves 25% of the node disk. After system use, NIC's 20 GiB default leaves roughly 2.4 GiB schedulable, so a 20 GiB Longhorn volume faults instead of provisioning. NIC can correct this through defaults or validation, but operators otherwise need to understand the hidden capacity rule.

a.xlink:title: Nebari should standardize the RWX contract and acceptance criteria while allowing each infrastructure provider to supply the implementation.

a.xlink:title: Shapes using managed RWX do not depend on FSx. EFS avoids a new integration, while FSx has a modeled recurring-cost advantage: $122-$1,127 per month at 50 users and $814-$4,834 per month at 200 users. FSx must recover its one-time integration and continuing maintenance cost across the expected cluster fleet and lifetime; EFS must not accumulate more recurring cost over that period than the integration work it avoids. The ranges remain uncertain because shared-storage I/O and EFS lifecycle tiering are not measured.

a.xlink:title: DSP already snapshots the workspace at launch rather than live-mounting it. A `nebi-pull` init container runs `nebi pull` and `pixi install` into a per-pod `emptyDir` at `/tmp/nebi-env`, and `NEBI_DATA_DIR` points every app pod at its own Nebi database, so a selected environment is re-materialized per pod rather than read from a shared filesystem. Every spawn still mounts the per-user RWO workspace PVC at `/var/lib/nebi/workspaces`, which the JupyterLab pod uses as its materialized-environment store, so that mount remains a second contributor to the node pin alongside home. Per-pod materialization exists to stop concurrent apps overwriting one another's manifest and Nebi database, not to relieve node pinning, so it survives a move to RWX homes: cross-node concurrent writes to one manifest and one SQLite file would make that conflict worse rather than better. Two live RWO mounts therefore remain on every spawn, home and the workspace store, and together they are why DSP pins app pods to the JupyterLab pod's node.

a.xlink:title: What both pods require is a way to obtain an environment, not a shared volume. Delivering materialized environments as prebuilt images, the same mechanism proposed for Ray workers, removes the environment store from the sharing question entirely. It leaves two narrower requirements: a writable local store for environments a user mutates during a session, which need not be shared or survive a node change, and a volume for authored files, which images do not carry but Nebi spec bundles can carry through their optional source layers. Kernel discovery reads the workspaces directory, so an image-per-environment model also implies selecting an environment at spawn rather than switching kernels in a session.

a.xlink:title: Pointing `NEBI_DATA_DIR` at node-local ephemeral storage keeps every client's database off the network filesystem, which is the correctness fix; DSP already does this for jhub-apps pods. Server mode is what makes the relocation lossless: workspace tracking moves behind one server process that keeps its own database on its own volume, so a discarded local database is a cache miss rather than lost state. SQLite remains the server default; PostgreSQL on CNPG is a separate availability and scale choice rather than a condition of the fix. DSP already runs Keycloak for OIDC. Nebi is alpha and explicitly not recommended for production use, so adopting and validating server mode remains a cost, and whether a client in server mode still keeps a local database needs confirmation against Nebi's own source.

a.xlink:title: The managed design trades per-volume machinery for a broader managed-service dependency.

EFS access points and FSx child volumes expose different quota, resize, snapshot, and deletion behavior. For FSx, child volumes can be quota-limited or share a growable parent pool but cannot combine a hard quota with in-place growth; the filesystem grows by at least 10%, has a six-hour cooldown, and never shrinks. Each candidate needs its own StorageClass and lifecycle contract.
